items.stem: Define the term 'corporate strategy'.
items.answer: A long-term plan of action for the whole organisation, designed to achieve its corporate objectives, e.g. which markets to compete in and how to grow.
items.markingKey: 2 marks: full definition, a long-term plan of action for the whole organisation, designed to achieve its corporate objectives, e.g. which markets to compete in and how to grow. 1 mark: partial definition or relevant example only. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between strategy and tactics.
items.answer: Strategy is the long-term plan to achieve corporate objectives, made by senior managers; tactics are short-term actions, often by middle managers, to carry out the strategy.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each. [2]

items.stem: Explain why a competitive advantage based on low prices may not last.
items.answer: Competitors can cut prices too, starting a price war; only a genuine cost advantage (e.g. economies of scale) can sustain low prices profitably.
items.markingKey: 1 mark rivals copy; 1 mark need for cost advantage. [2]

items.stem: Based in Hanoi, Mekong Furniture JSC (joint stock company) makes wooden and rattan furniture for large retailers in the USA and Europe. The business has around 1,200 employees. A major US retailer has asked it to cut delivery times from twelve weeks to six. Explain why Mekong Furniture needs both a clear strategy and effective tactics.
items.answer: Points to develop for Mekong Furniture: strategy sets long-term direction; tactics turn strategy into action; poor tactics can undermine a good strategy; tactics must be coordinated across departments.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [1]: strategy sets long-term direction. AO2 Application [1]: answer uses the case (Mekong Furniture: furniture manufacturing, about 1,200 employees, joint stock company in Vietnam; a major US retailer has asked it to cut delivery times from twelve weeks to six). AO3 Analysis [2]: developed chains of reasoning showing the consequence for Mekong Furniture, e.g. tactics turn strategy into action; poor tactics can undermine a good strategy; tactics must be coordinated across departments. Levels: L1 knowledge only; L2 applied to the case; L3 applied and analysed. [4]

items.stem: The founder is retiring and the new managing director wants to modernise production. Andes Textil SA, a family-owned private company in Peru with about 320 employees, makes premium alpaca knitwear for fashion retailers in North America and Japan. Explain how Andes Textil could build a sustainable competitive advantage.
items.answer: Points to develop for Andes Textil: competitive advantage allows the firm to outperform rivals; cost leadership through scale or efficiency; differentiation through brand, quality or innovation of alpaca knitwear; core competencies that rivals cannot copy.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [1]: competitive advantage allows the firm to outperform rivals. AO2 Application [1]: answer uses the case (Andes Textil: textile manufacturing, about 320 employees, family-owned private company in Peru; the founder is retiring and the new managing director wants to modernise production). AO3 Analysis [2]: developed chains of reasoning showing the consequence for Andes Textil, e.g. cost leadership through scale or efficiency; differentiation through brand, quality or innovation of alpaca knitwear; core competencies that rivals cannot copy. Levels: L1 knowledge only; L2 applied to the case; L3 applied and analysed. [4]

items.stem: Large customers are asking for real-time tracking of every delivery. Pearl Logistics WLL, a private limited company in Qatar with about 1,500 employees, provides freight forwarding, warehousing and lorry delivery services. Evaluate the most important source of competitive advantage for Pearl Logistics.
items.answer: For: low costs; brand and reputation; innovation and core competencies. Against: costs can be matched by rivals; brands take time and money; innovation can be copied. Judgement: the decision for Pearl Logistics depends mainly on the nature of its market, and also on its resources and capabilities.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [2]: relevant concepts/theory. AO2 Application [2]: uses case evidence (Pearl Logistics: logistics, about 1,500 employees, private limited company in Qatar; large customers are asking for real-time tracking of every delivery). AO3 Analysis [4]: arguments for, e.g. low costs; brand and reputation; innovation and core competencies; arguments against, e.g. costs can be matched by rivals; brands take time and money; innovation can be copied. AO4 Evaluation [4]: a supported judgement that weighs the arguments, e.g. it depends on the nature of its market; its resources and capabilities; what customers value most. Highest level needs a justified conclusion specific to Pearl Logistics, not a generic one. [12]

items.stem: Lumen Robotics plc is a public limited company based in Singapore. It designs and builds robots used on factory assembly lines and employs about 2,400 people. Shareholders are pressing for higher dividends while engineers want more spending on research. Explain one disadvantage to Lumen Robotics of developing a formal long-term corporate strategy.
items.answer: Time-consuming to prepare.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: relevant disadvantage, e.g. time-consuming to prepare; can become inflexible; depends on accurate analysis of the future. 1 mark: explained in the context of Lumen Robotics (industrial engineering). [2]

items.answer: Points to develop for Mekong Furniture: competitive advantage allows the firm to outperform rivals; cost leadership through scale or efficiency; differentiation through brand, quality or innovation of wooden furniture; core competencies that rivals cannot copy.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [1]: competitive advantage allows the firm to outperform rivals. items.stem: Demand has grown faster than its small brewery can produce. Cape Brew Co. (Pty) Ltd, a private limited company in South Africa with about 140 employees, brews craft beers and low-sugar soft drinks sold through bars and supermarkets. Explain why Cape Brew needs both a clear strategy and effective tactics, and judge which point is most important for Cape Brew.
items.answer: Points to develop for Cape Brew: strategy sets long-term direction; tactics turn strategy into action; poor tactics can undermine a good strategy; tactics must be coordinated across departments.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [1]: strategy sets long-term direction. AO2 Application [1]: answer uses the case (Cape Brew: beverages, about 140 employees, private limited company in South Africa; demand has grown faster than its small brewery can produce). AO3 Analysis [2]: developed chains of reasoning showing the consequence for Cape Brew, e.g. tactics turn strategy into action; poor tactics can undermine a good strategy; tactics must be coordinated across departments. Levels: L1 knowledge only; L2 applied to the case; L3 applied and analysed. [4]

items.stem: Define the term 'SWOT analysis'.
items.answer: A strategic analysis tool that identifies a business's internal strengths and weaknesses and the external opportunities and threats it faces.
items.markingKey: 2 marks: full definition, a strategic analysis tool that identifies a business's internal strengths and weaknesses and the external opportunities and threats it faces. 1 mark: partial definition or relevant example only. [2]

items.stem: Explain how a business can use the results of a SWOT analysis to develop a strategy.
items.answer: It can use strengths to exploit opportunities, address weaknesses that limit it, and plan to counter threats, e.g. by matching a strong brand to a growing market.
items.markingKey: 1 mark matching S to O; 1 mark addressing W/T. [2]

items.stem: Explain why PESTLE analysis is important for a business planning to enter a new country.
items.answer: Political stability, economic conditions, culture, technology, laws and environment differ by country and determine the risks and opportunities of entry.
items.markingKey: 1 mark external factors differ; 1 mark effect on risk/opportunity. [2]

items.stem: Based in Dubai, Desert Bloom Hotels plc (public limited company) operates fourteen four- and five-star hotels. The business has around 3,100 employees. Occupancy rates have fallen since two new rival hotels opened nearby. Explain two external threats that a PESTLE analysis might identify for Desert Bloom.
items.answer: Points to develop for Desert Bloom: PESTLE examines external factors; economic: recession or rising interest rates reduce demand for hotel rooms and conference facilities; legal/environmental: stricter regulation raises costs; technological: new technology could make products obsolete.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [1]: PESTLE examines external factors. AO2 Application [1]: answer uses the case (Desert Bloom: hospitality, about 3,100 employees, public limited company in the United Arab Emirates; occupancy rates have fallen since two new rival hotels opened nearby). AO3 Analysis [2]: developed chains of reasoning showing the consequence for Desert Bloom, e.g. economic: recession or rising interest rates reduce demand for hotel rooms and conference facilities; legal/environmental: stricter regulation raises costs; technological: new technology could make products obsolete. Levels: L1 knowledge only; L2 applied to the case; L3 applied and analysed. [4]

items.stem: Lanka Tea Estates plc is a public limited company based in Colombo, Sri Lanka. It grows, processes and packs tea on its own estates and employs about 5,000 people. Many young workers are leaving the estates for jobs in the cities. Explain two external threats that a PESTLE analysis might identify for Lanka Tea.
items.answer: Points to develop for Lanka Tea: PESTLE examines external factors; economic: recession or rising interest rates reduce demand for packaged tea; legal/environmental: stricter regulation raises costs; technological: new technology could make products obsolete.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [1]: PESTLE examines external factors. AO2 Application [1]: answer uses the case (Lanka Tea: agriculture and food, about 5,000 employees, public limited company in Sri Lanka; many young workers are leaving the estates for jobs in the cities). AO3 Analysis [2]: developed chains of reasoning showing the consequence for Lanka Tea, e.g. economic: recession or rising interest rates reduce demand for packaged tea; legal/environmental: stricter regulation raises costs; technological: new technology could make products obsolete. Levels: L1 knowledge only; L2 applied to the case; L3 applied and analysed. [4]

items.stem: Based in Manila, IslaConnect Inc. (private limited company) runs customer-service call centres for banks and airlines in the USA and Australia. The business has around 2,600 employees. Clients are starting to replace human call handlers with artificial intelligence. Explain how IslaConnect could use a SWOT analysis to decide whether to launch AI chatbot services.
items.answer: Points to develop for IslaConnect: SWOT identifies internal and external factors; strengths such as brand or skills support the launch; weaknesses such as limited finance increase risk; opportunities and threats in the target market.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [1]: SWOT identifies internal and external factors. AO2 Application [1]: answer uses the case (IslaConnect: business process outsourcing, about 2,600 employees, private limited company in the Philippines; clients are starting to replace human call handlers with artificial intelligence). AO3 Analysis [2]: developed chains of reasoning showing the consequence for IslaConnect, e.g. strengths such as brand or skills support the launch; weaknesses such as limited finance increase risk; opportunities and threats in the target market. Levels: L1 knowledge only; L2 applied to the case; L3 applied and analysed. [4]

items.stem: Based in Dubai, Desert Bloom Hotels plc (public limited company) operates fourteen four- and five-star hotels. The business has around 3,100 employees. Occupancy rates have fallen since two new rival hotels opened nearby. Evaluate the usefulness of SWOT analysis to Desert Bloom when planning its future strategy.
items.answer: For: structured overview; links internal capabilities to the environment; simple and cheap. Against: subjective and static; does not prioritise; needs other tools such as Porter or Ansoff. Judgement: the decision for Desert Bloom depends mainly on the quality of the information used, and also on how often it is updated.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [2]: relevant concepts/theory. AO2 Application [2]: uses case evidence (Desert Bloom: hospitality, about 3,100 employees, public limited company in the United Arab Emirates; occupancy rates have fallen since two new rival hotels opened nearby). AO3 Analysis [4]: arguments for, e.g. structured overview; links internal capabilities to the environment; simple and cheap; arguments against, e.g. subjective and static; does not prioritise; needs other tools such as Porter or Ansoff. AO4 Evaluation [4]: a supported judgement that weighs the arguments, e.g. it depends on the quality of the information used; how often it is updated; whether it leads to action. Highest level needs a justified conclusion specific to Desert Bloom, not a generic one. [12]

items.stem: Based in Cairo, Nile Pharma plc (public limited company) manufactures generic medicines for hospitals and pharmacies in Africa and the Middle East. The business has around 1,800 employees. Most of its raw ingredients are imported and paid for in US dollars. Evaluate the usefulness of SWOT analysis to Nile Pharma when planning its future strategy.
items.answer: For: structured overview; links internal capabilities to the environment; simple and cheap. Against: subjective and static; does not prioritise; needs other tools such as Porter or Ansoff. Judgement: the decision for Nile Pharma depends mainly on the quality of the information used, and also on how often it is updated.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [3]: relevant concepts/theory. AO2 Application [3]: uses case evidence (Nile Pharma: pharmaceuticals, about 1,800 employees, public limited company in Egypt; most of its raw ingredients are imported and paid for in US dollars). AO3 Analysis [5]: arguments for, e.g. structured overview; links internal capabilities to the environment; simple and cheap; arguments against, e.g. subjective and static; does not prioritise; needs other tools such as Porter or Ansoff. AO4 Evaluation [5]: a supported judgement that weighs the arguments, e.g. it depends on the quality of the information used; how often it is updated; whether it leads to action. Highest level needs a justified conclusion specific to Nile Pharma, not a generic one. [16]

items.stem: In SWOT analysis, which elements are internal to the business?
items.answer: Strengths and weaknesses
items.markingKey: Strengths and weaknesses. S and W are internal; O and T are external.

items.stem: Which of the following best defines 'external environment'?
options: A product's market share divided by the market share of its largest competitor.
The process of analysing the business and its environment, choosing a strategy and implementing and reviewing it to achieve long-term objectives.
The first stage of strategic management: researching and analysing the business and its environment to understand its current position.
Factors outside the control of the business, such as the economy, competitors, laws and technology, that affect its performance.
items.answer: Factors outside the control of the business, such as the economy, competitors, laws and technology, that affect its performance.
items.markingKey: external environment: Factors outside the control of the business, such as the economy, competitors, laws and technology, that affect its performance.

items.stem: Explain two limitations of PESTLE analysis.
items.answer: Factors change quickly so analysis dates; it may be subjective; it can produce long lists without showing which factors matter most.
items.markingKey: 2 × (1 mark limitation, 1 mark explanation). [4]

items.stem: Online sales are growing quickly while sales in its high-street stores are falling. Iberia Moda SA, a public limited company in Spain with about 6,000 employees, runs 180 fast-fashion clothing stores and an online shop. A consultant lists these factors for Iberia Moda: (1) stricter environmental regulations; (2) dependence on one main customer; (3) a government subsidy for green investment; (4) high labour turnover among managers. Classify each factor in a SWOT analysis.
items.answer: (1) Threat; (2) Weakness; (3) Opportunity; (4) Weakness
items.markingKey: (1) Threat; (2) Weakness; (3) Opportunity; (4) Weakness — ½ mark each, rounded [2]. [2]

items.stem: A global brand has threatened to cancel its contract after a report on long working hours. Nusantara Apparel Tbk, a public limited company in Indonesia with about 4,000 employees, makes sportswear under contract for global brands. Evaluate the usefulness of SWOT analysis to Nusantara Apparel when planning its future strategy.
items.answer: For: structured overview; links internal capabilities to the environment; simple and cheap. Judgement: the decision for Nusantara Apparel depends mainly on the quality of the information used, and also on how often it is updated.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [2]: relevant concepts/theory. items.stem: Define the term 'Porter's five forces'.
items.answer: A model for analysing the competitive environment of an industry using five forces: threat of new entrants, power of buyers, power of suppliers, threat of substitutes and competitive rivalry.
items.markingKey: 2 marks: full definition, a model for analysing the competitive environment of an industry using five forces: threat of new entrants, power of buyers, power of suppliers, threat of substitutes and competitive rivalry. 1 mark: partial definition or relevant example only. [2]

items.stem: Explain how high barriers to entry benefit existing firms in a market.
items.answer: Fewer new rivals can enter, so competition is limited and existing firms can keep higher prices and profits.
items.markingKey: 1 mark fewer entrants; 1 mark higher prices/profits. [2]

items.stem: Explain why core competencies can give a sustainable competitive advantage.
items.answer: They are hard for rivals to copy because they combine skills, knowledge and culture built up over time, and they can be used to enter several markets.
items.markingKey: 1 mark hard to copy; 1 mark applicable across markets/value to customers. [2]

items.stem: The founder is retiring and the new managing director wants to modernise production. Andes Textil SA, a family-owned private company in Peru with about 320 employees, makes premium alpaca knitwear for fashion retailers in North America and Japan. Explain how Porter's five forces could help Andes Textil understand the competitive pressures in its industry.
items.answer: Points to develop for Andes Textil: five forces analyse industry competition; buyer and supplier power affect prices and margins; threat of entrants and substitutes limits pricing; rivalry determines intensity of competition.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [1]: five forces analyse industry competition. AO2 Application [1]: answer uses the case (Andes Textil: textile manufacturing, about 320 employees, family-owned private company in Peru; the founder is retiring and the new managing director wants to modernise production). AO3 Analysis [2]: developed chains of reasoning showing the consequence for Andes Textil, e.g. buyer and supplier power affect prices and margins; threat of entrants and substitutes limits pricing; rivalry determines intensity of competition. Levels: L1 knowledge only; L2 applied to the case; L3 applied and analysed. [4]

items.stem: Its largest European customer has just demanded lower prices and proof of sustainable water use. Savanna Fresh Ltd, a private limited company in Kenya with about 850 employees, grows cut flowers and green beans and exports them by air to supermarkets in Europe. Explain how Savanna Fresh could use its core competencies to grow.
items.answer: Points to develop for Savanna Fresh: core competencies are unique, hard-to-copy capabilities; apply them to new products such as ready-to-eat salad packs; enter new markets using existing strengths; reduce risk compared with unrelated diversification.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [1]: core competencies are unique, hard-to-copy capabilities. AO2 Application [1]: answer uses the case (Savanna Fresh: horticulture, about 850 employees, private limited company in Kenya; its largest European customer has just demanded lower prices and proof of sustainable water use). AO3 Analysis [2]: developed chains of reasoning showing the consequence for Savanna Fresh, e.g. apply them to new products such as ready-to-eat salad packs; enter new markets using existing strengths; reduce risk compared with unrelated diversification. Levels: L1 knowledge only; L2 applied to the case; L3 applied and analysed. [4]

items.stem: One game earns 70% of its revenue and its popularity is starting to fall. Han River Games Co., a private limited company in South Korea with about 340 employees, develops mobile games that earn revenue from in-game purchases. Discuss whether Han River Games should build its strategy around its core competencies.
items.answer: For: sustainable advantage; basis for related growth; efficient use of resources. Against: competencies may become obsolete; may limit vision; hard to identify objectively. Judgement: the decision for Han River Games depends mainly on the pace of technological change, and also on how unique its competencies are.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [2]: relevant concepts/theory. AO2 Application [2]: uses case evidence (Han River Games: video game development, about 340 employees, private limited company in South Korea; one game earns 70% of its revenue and its popularity is starting to fall). AO3 Analysis [4]: arguments for, e.g. sustainable advantage; basis for related growth; efficient use of resources; arguments against, e.g. competencies may become obsolete; may limit vision; hard to identify objectively. AO4 Evaluation [4]: a supported judgement that weighs the arguments, e.g. it depends on the pace of technological change; how unique its competencies are; market opportunities. Highest level needs a justified conclusion specific to Han River Games, not a generic one. [12]

items.stem: Andina Solar SpA is a private limited company based in Santiago, Chile. It designs and installs solar power systems for farms, mines and homes and employs about 380 people. The government has announced new subsidies for business investment in renewable energy. Explain one advantage to Andina Solar of focusing on its core competencies and outsourcing other activities.
items.answer: Resources concentrated on what it does best.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: relevant advantage, e.g. resources concentrated on what it does best; lower costs through specialist suppliers; stronger competitive advantage. 1 mark: explained in the context of Andina Solar (renewable energy). [2]

items.stem: Based in Lisbon, Tejo Mobility SA (public limited company) assembles electric scooters and e-bikes for sale across the European Union. The business has around 600 employees. Battery supply problems from Asia have delayed several large orders. Explain how Porter's five forces could help Tejo Mobility understand the competitive pressures in its industry.
items.answer: Points to develop for Tejo Mobility: five forces analyse industry competition; buyer and supplier power affect prices and margins; threat of entrants and substitutes limits pricing; rivalry determines intensity of competition.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [1]: five forces analyse industry competition. AO2 Application [1]: answer uses the case (Tejo Mobility: vehicle manufacturing, about 600 employees, public limited company in Portugal; battery supply problems from Asia have delayed several large orders). AO3 Analysis [2]: developed chains of reasoning showing the consequence for Tejo Mobility, e.g. buyer and supplier power affect prices and margins; threat of entrants and substitutes limits pricing; rivalry determines intensity of competition. Levels: L1 knowledge only; L2 applied to the case; L3 applied and analysed. [4]

items.stem: Based in Muscat, Muscat Dates & Co. LLC (family-owned limited company) processes, packs and exports dates and date syrup. The business has around 160 employees. Three family members disagree about whether to sell shares to an outside investor. Using the case and your own knowledge, evaluate the usefulness of Porter's five forces model to Muscat Dates when deciding whether to enter a new market.
items.answer: For: identifies competitive pressures; shows likely profitability; highlights barriers. Against: static snapshot; difficult to measure forces; ignores the firm's own competencies. Judgement: the decision for Muscat Dates depends mainly on how quickly the market is changing, and also on the quality of information.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [3]: relevant concepts/theory. AO2 Application [3]: uses case evidence (Muscat Dates: food processing, about 160 employees, family-owned limited company in Oman; three family members disagree about whether to sell shares to an outside investor). AO4 Evaluation [5]: a supported judgement that weighs the arguments, e.g. it depends on how quickly the market is changing; the quality of information; use with SWOT and Ansoff. Highest level needs a justified conclusion specific to Muscat Dates, not a generic one. [16]

items.stem: Define the term 'Boston matrix'.
items.answer: A model that classifies a firm's products or business units by market growth rate and relative market share into stars, cash cows, question marks (problem children) and dogs.
items.markingKey: 2 marks: full definition, a model that classifies a firm's products or business units by market growth rate and relative market share into stars, cash cows, question marks (problem children) and dogs. 1 mark: partial definition or relevant example only. [2]

items.stem: Explain how a business can use the Boston matrix to manage its product portfolio.
items.answer: It shows the balance of products: cash cows generate funds that can be invested in stars and selected question marks, while weak dogs may be dropped.
items.markingKey: 1 mark classification; 1 mark resource allocation decisions. [2]

items.stem: Explain why a business needs a balanced product portfolio.
items.answer: Products at different stages generate and use cash differently; a balance ensures current cash flow and future growth and spreads risk.
items.markingKey: 1 mark cash generation/use; 1 mark growth/risk. [2]

items.stem: Venture capital investors expect it to become profitable within two years. Maple Learning Inc., a private limited company in Canada with about 260 employees, runs an online tutoring and test-preparation platform for school students. Explain the risks to Maple Learning of having most of its sales from one cash cow product.
items.answer: Points to develop for Maple Learning: cash cows are in low-growth markets; decline could sharply reduce revenue; few stars to replace it; need to develop new products such as a teacher-training platform for schools.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [1]: cash cows are in low-growth markets. AO2 Application [1]: answer uses the case (Maple Learning: education technology, about 260 employees, private limited company in Canada; venture capital investors expect it to become profitable within two years). AO3 Analysis [2]: developed chains of reasoning showing the consequence for Maple Learning, e.g. decline could sharply reduce revenue; few stars to replace it; need to develop new products such as a teacher-training platform for schools. Levels: L1 knowledge only; L2 applied to the case; L3 applied and analysed. [4]

items.stem: Based in Auckland, Kiwi Trails Ltd (private limited company) runs guided hiking, kayaking and cycling tours. The business has around 90 employees. Bookings are highly seasonal and most guides are employed only for the summer. Explain how Kiwi Trails could use the Boston matrix to allocate its marketing budget.
items.answer: Points to develop for Kiwi Trails: Boston matrix classifies by growth and relative share; build question marks with potential; hold and milk cash cows; harvest or divest dogs.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [1]: Boston matrix classifies by growth and relative share. AO2 Application [1]: answer uses the case (Kiwi Trails: tourism, about 90 employees, private limited company in New Zealand; bookings are highly seasonal and most guides are employed only for the summer). AO3 Analysis [2]: developed chains of reasoning showing the consequence for Kiwi Trails, e.g. build question marks with potential; hold and milk cash cows; harvest or divest dogs. Levels: L1 knowledge only; L2 applied to the case; L3 applied and analysed. [4]

items.stem: A rival in China has started selling machine-made balls at lower prices. Indus Sports Goods Ltd, a private limited company in Pakistan with about 950 employees, makes hand-stitched and machine-stitched footballs and cricket equipment. Discuss whether Indus Sports should withdraw its products classified as dogs.
items.answer: For: frees resources; simplifies range; focus on stars. Against: may still make positive contribution; support other products; loyal customers. Judgement: the decision for Indus Sports depends mainly on their contribution, and also on links with other products.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [2]: relevant concepts/theory. AO2 Application [2]: uses case evidence (Indus Sports: sports equipment manufacturing, about 950 employees, private limited company in Pakistan; a rival in China has started selling machine-made balls at lower prices). AO3 Analysis [4]: arguments for, e.g. frees resources; simplifies range; focus on stars; arguments against, e.g. may still make positive contribution; support other products; loyal customers. AO4 Evaluation [4]: a supported judgement that weighs the arguments, e.g. it depends on their contribution; links with other products; cost of withdrawal. Highest level needs a justified conclusion specific to Indus Sports, not a generic one. [12]

items.stem: Explain why a "dog" product might not be withdrawn.
items.answer: It may still make a positive contribution, support sales of other products, or have loyal customers; withdrawal could also harm brand image.
items.markingKey: 1 mark reason; 1 mark explanation. [2]

items.stem: Gold Coast Cocoa Ltd has three product lines — P1: market growth 3% a year, own share 30%, largest rival 20%; P2: market growth 2% a year, own share 25%, largest rival 30%; P3: market growth 3% a year, own share 35%, largest rival 40%. Taking high growth as 10% or more, calculate the relative market share of each and classify it using the Boston matrix.
items.answer: P1 1.5 Cash cow; P2 0.83 Dog; P3 0.88 Dog

items.stem: Indus Sports Goods Ltd is a private limited company based in Karachi, Pakistan. It makes hand-stitched and machine-stitched footballs and cricket equipment and employs about 950 people. A rival in China has started selling machine-made balls at lower prices. Using the case and your own knowledge, evaluate the usefulness of the Boston matrix to Indus Sports in planning its product strategy.
items.answer: For: simple visual tool; shows balance and cash needs; helps allocate resources. Against: only two variables; ignores profitability; snapshot that changes. Judgement: the decision for Indus Sports depends mainly on how markets are defined, and also on availability of market data.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [3]: relevant concepts/theory. AO2 Application [3]: uses case evidence (Indus Sports: sports equipment manufacturing, about 950 employees, private limited company in Pakistan; a rival in China has started selling machine-made balls at lower prices). AO4 Evaluation [5]: a supported judgement that weighs the arguments, e.g. it depends on how markets are defined; availability of market data; use with product life cycle and Ansoff. Highest level needs a justified conclusion specific to Indus Sports, not a generic one. [16]

items.stem: Which is an example of a strategic decision rather than a tactical one?
options: Changing the price of one product for a weekend
items.answer: Entering a new overseas market
items.markingKey: Entering a new overseas market. Strategic decisions are long-term, high-risk and affect the whole business.

items.stem: Explain why strategic decisions are usually made by senior managers.
items.answer: They commit large resources, are long-term, hard to reverse and affect the whole organisation, so they need the overview and authority of senior management.
items.markingKey: 1 mark characteristics; 1 mark link to senior managers. [2]

items.stem: Based in Kuala Lumpur, BatikPay Sdn Bhd (private limited company) runs a mobile payments app used by 4 million customers and 90 000 small shops. The business has around 210 employees. The central bank has announced tighter rules on data protection for payment apps. Explain how BatikPay could build a sustainable competitive advantage.

items.stem: Which of the following best defines 'competitive advantage'?
options: A feature or capability that allows a business to outperform its rivals, by offering better value through lower prices or greater benefits.
A unique combination of skills, knowledge and technology that gives a business a competitive advantage, can be applied to many markets and is hard to copy (Prahalad and Hamel).
A model that classifies a firm's products or business units by market growth rate and relative market share into stars, cash cows, question marks (problem children) and dogs.
The process of analysing the business and its environment, choosing a strategy and implementing and reviewing it to achieve long-term objectives.
items.answer: A feature or capability that allows a business to outperform its rivals, by offering better value through lower prices or greater benefits.
